subject: python
title: Python Foundations
subtitle: From your first line of code to writing programs that actually do something.
description: A twelve-week course that takes a complete beginner to the point of writing real programs. Every lesson pairs a short explanation with code you run yourself, and every week ends with a live class where you can ask the thing you did not want to ask in front of your class at school.
outcomes: Write and run Python programs on your own machine
Use variables, conditions and loops without looking them up
Read an error message and know what to do about it
Build a small project from a blank file

modules.title: Getting started
modules.summary: What a program is, and how to make the computer do something.

body.text: A program is a list of instructions

The computer does exactly what you write, in the order you write it. That is the whole idea, and it is also why programming is frustrating at first: the computer is never wrong about what you asked, only about what you meant.
print() puts something on the screen. The brackets hold what you want printed, and text goes in quotes.
If you see a red error mentioning a quote, you probably opened one and forgot to close it.

exercises.title: Print your own name
exercises.brief: Print your name on the screen. One line is enough.
hints: print() puts something on the screen

tests.name: prints something
tests.hint: Use print() so we can see your answer.

body.text: A name for a value
When you write age = 14, Python stores 14 and lets you reach it again by the name age. The name is not the value; it points at the value.
Names that make code readable

items: Use lowercase with underscores: total_marks, not TM
A name cannot start with a number
Choose a name that says what it holds

exercises.title: Swap two values
exercises.brief: Two variables a and b are given. Print them, swap them, then print them again.
exercises.starter:
a = 3
b = 8

# print, swap, print again
hints: Python can do a, b = b, a in one line
Or use a third variable to hold one of them
exercises.solution:
a = 3
b = 8
print(a, b)
a, b = b, a
print(a, b)

body.text: Four types you will use constantly

items: int — a whole number, like 14
float — a number with a decimal point, like 14.5
str — text, always in quotes
bool — True or False, with capital letters

body.source:
print(type(5))      # <class 'int'>
print(type(5.0))    # <class 'float'>
print(type("5"))    # <class 'str'>
print(5 / 2)        # 2.5  — division always gives a float

body.text: When something behaves strangely, print the type first. It is the fastest way to find the problem.

modules.title: Input and decisions
modules.summary: Programs that ask questions and choose what to do.

body.text: The rule to remember
input() always gives you text. Even when the person types 25, Python holds the characters "2" and "5", not the number twenty-five.

body.source:
age = input("Your age? ")
print(age + 1)      # this breaks
print(int(age) + 1) # this works

body.text: Three things that go wrong

items: Adding to text instead of a number, so 25 + 1 becomes an error
Forgetting the space at the end of the question, so the answer sticks to it
Using int() on something that is not a number at all

body.text: int("twenty five") will not work. int() only converts text that looks like a number.

exercises.title: Add two numbers the user types
exercises.brief: Ask for two numbers and print their total. Remember what input() gives you back.
exercises.starter:
a = input("First number: ")
b = input("Second number: ")

# print the total
hints: input() gives text, not a number
exercises.solution:
a = input("First number: ")
b = input("Second number: ")
print(int(a) + int(b))

tests.name: 25 and 17 make 42
tests.hint: If you saw 2517, you joined the text instead of adding the numbers.

body.text: Choosing between paths
elif only runs when every condition above it was false. else runs when none of them were true.
Indentation is not decoration
The spaces at the start of a line tell Python which lines belong inside the if. Four spaces is the convention. Mixing tabs and spaces is the commonest first-week error.

exercises.title: Biggest of three numbers
exercises.brief: Read three numbers and print the biggest, using if and elif. Do not use max().
exercises.starter:
a = int(input())
b = int(input())
c = int(input())

# which is biggest?
hints: Compare a with b first, then the winner with c
if a > b and a > c:

tests.name: 4, 9, 2 gives 9
tests.hint: The task asks you to compare them yourself, without max().

modules.title: Loops and lists
modules.summary: Doing something many times, and holding many things at once.

body.text: Two kinds of repetition
for repeats a fixed number of times. while repeats until something changes.
range(1, 11) gives you 1 to 10 — it stops before the second number, which surprises everyone once.
A while loop whose condition never becomes false runs forever. If your program hangs, that is why.

exercises.title: Times table using a loop
exercises.brief: Print the 5 times table from 5 x 1 to 5 x 10, one line each. Use a loop — not ten print lines.
exercises.starter: # Print the 5 times table using a loop
exercises.solution:
for i in range(1, 11):
    print(5, "x", i, "=", 5 * i)

tests.name: uses a loop
tests.hint: The task asks for a loop. Ten print lines will not pass.

tests.name: reaches 50
tests.hint: The last line should be 5 x 10 = 50.

body.text: Many values under one name

body.source:
marks = [78, 65, 90, 55, 82]
print(marks[0])      # 78 — counting starts at zero
print(len(marks))    # 5
marks.append(71)

body.text: Walking through a list

body.source:
total = 0
for m in marks:
    total = total + m
print("Average:", total / len(marks))

exercises.title: Count the even numbers
exercises.brief: Given the list below, print how many of the numbers are even.
hints: A number is even when n % 2 == 0
Keep a counter starting at 0 and add 1 each time

body.text: A program is a set of instructions written precisely enough that a machine can follow them without asking you what you meant.
That precision is the whole skill. Everything else — the syntax, the libraries, the tools — is detail you can look up.
Why Python

items: It reads close to English
It is used in real work, from science to web sites
The error messages tell you something useful

body.text: Open the editor, type one line, press Run. The output appears underneath.
You cannot break anything by running code. Try the wrong thing on purpose and read what it says.
A variable is a name that refers to a value. Assigning to it again points the name somewhere new; it does not change the old value.
int(), float() and str() move a value from one type to another. They do not change the original — they hand you a new value.
int() on text that is not a number raises ValueError. That is Python telling you the input was not what you assumed.

items: == is "equal to". A single = assigns.
!= is "not equal to"
< > <= >= work as you expect

body.text: and requires both sides to be true; or requires either. not flips a condition.

body.source:
if age >= 13 and consent == True:
    print("Can sign up")

quizzes.title: Unit 1 — Getting started
quizzes.description: Variables, types and printing. Ten minutes.

questions.text: What will print(type(5 / 2)) show in Python 3?
questions.explanation: Division always produces a float, even when the result is whole.

questions.text: Which line converts the text "25" into a number?
questions.explanation: int() converts text that looks like a whole number.

questions.text: Which is a valid variable name?
questions.explanation: Names cannot start with a digit or contain spaces or hyphens.

questions.text: What does print("5" + "5") show?
questions.explanation: Adding two strings joins them. Adding two numbers adds them.

questions.text: After score = 10 then score = score + 5, what is score?
questions.explanation: The right-hand side is worked out first, then assigned back to the name.

quizzes.title: Unit 2 — Input and decisions
quizzes.description: input(), if / elif / else and comparisons.

questions.text: What does input() always return?
options: Whatever the user typed, in its own type
questions.explanation: Always text. Convert it before doing arithmetic.

questions.text: In an if / elif / else chain, when does else run?
options: Only if every condition above was false
Only if the first was true
questions.explanation: else is the fallback when nothing above matched.

questions.text: What is the value of 7 % 2?
questions.explanation: % gives the remainder. 7 divided by 2 leaves 1.

questions.text: Which operator tests equality?
questions.explanation: A single = assigns; == compares.

questions.text: How many numbers does range(1, 11) produce?
questions.explanation: It starts at 1 and stops before 11, so 1 to 10.

questions.text: Which keyword starts a loop that runs a fixed number of times?
questions.explanation: for iterates a known number of times; while repeats until a condition changes.

questions.text: For marks = [78, 65, 90], what is marks[0]?
questions.explanation: Counting starts at zero.

questions.text: What is the commonest cause of a program that never finishes?
options: A while condition that never becomes false
questions.explanation: If nothing inside the loop changes the condition, it runs forever.

subject: ai
title: Artificial Intelligence for Beginners
subtitle: What AI actually is, how it learns from data, and where it goes wrong.
description: An eight-week introduction to artificial intelligence for students who have never trained a model. No heavy mathematics. You will work with real data, build a simple classifier, and finish able to explain why an AI system made a decision — and when you should not trust it.
outcomes: Explain what makes a system "AI" rather than ordinary software
Take a dataset from messy to usable
Train and evaluate a simple model
Spot bias in data before it becomes bias in a decision

modules.title: What AI is
modules.summary: Definitions that survive contact with reality.

body.text: The one distinction that matters
Ordinary software follows rules a person wrote. An AI system finds the rules itself, from examples. That is the whole difference, and everything else follows from it.
It also explains the failure mode: a model learns the world it was shown, including the parts of that world nobody meant to teach it.

items: Spam filters learn from mail people marked as spam
Recommendation systems learn from what people watched
A face recogniser learns from the faces it was given

body.text: Five stages, in order

items: Problem scoping — who has the problem, and what counts as solving it
Data acquisition — where the data comes from, and with whose permission
Data exploration — looking before modelling
Modelling — the part everyone thinks is the whole job
Evaluation — does it work for the people it was built for

body.text: If you cannot write the problem statement in one sentence, you are not ready to collect data.

modules.title: Working with data
modules.summary: Most of a real project is here.

body.text: Primary and secondary
Primary data you collect yourself. Secondary data someone else collected, for their own purpose — which is why it rarely fits yours exactly.
Consent is not optional
If the data is about people, they need to know it is being collected and what for. That applies to a school project as much as to a company.
The three problems you will always find

items: Missing values — a blank is not a zero
Duplicates — the same person recorded twice
Impossible values — an age of 250

body.source:
import statistics

ages = [12, 13, None, 14, 250, 13]
clean = [a for a in ages if a is not None and 0 < a < 120]
print(clean)
print("median:", statistics.median(clean))

body.text: Never silently delete a row you do not understand. Record what you removed and why.

exercises.title: Remove the impossible ages
exercises.brief: The list has a missing value and one impossible age. Print the cleaned list.
exercises.starter:
ages = [12, 13, None, 14, 250, 13]

# print only the sensible ages
hints: Check for None first, then check the range
A loop with an if inside works fine

tests.name: drops the impossible age
tests.hint: Print the cleaned list, not the original.

modules.title: Statistics you actually need
modules.summary: Enough to read a result honestly.

body.text: Three answers to one question

items: Mean — add everything, divide by how many. Moves when one value is extreme.
Median — put them in order, take the middle. Barely moves.
Mode — the value appearing most often. Useful for categories.

body.text: Why it matters
Marks: 12, 14, 15, 16, 98. The mean is 31, which describes nobody. The median is 15, which describes almost everyone. One unusual value dragged the mean away from the truth.

exercises.title: Mean and median
exercises.brief: Print the mean and the median of the marks list. You may use the statistics module.
exercises.starter:
marks = [12, 14, 15, 16, 98]

# print the mean, then the median
hints: import statistics gives you statistics.mean and statistics.median
Or compute the mean with sum(marks) / len(marks)

lessons.title: Reading a chart without being fooled

body.text: Read the scale before the shape
A bar chart whose axis starts at 90 rather than 0 makes a two-point difference look enormous. Check the axis first, every time.

items: Bar — comparing separate groups
Line — something changing over time
Pie — parts of one whole, and only when there are few parts

modules.title: Bias and responsibility
modules.summary: The part that decides whether the system should be built at all.

body.text: It is almost never the algorithm
A model reproduces the pattern in its training data. If the data under-represents a group, the model works worse for that group — and it will do so confidently, which is what makes it dangerous.
Questions to ask before trusting a prediction

items: Who is in the training data, and who is missing?
Who checked the result for the people it affects?
What happens to someone the model gets wrong?

body.text: The clearest test: could a person have written down the rule? If yes, it is ordinary software. If the rule was found in data, it is machine learning.

items: A calculator follows rules
A spam filter learned them
A thermostat follows rules; a smart thermostat learned your habits

body.text: Search suggestions, photo tagging, route prediction, video recommendations, voice assistants. You interact with several before breakfast.
Pick one you used today and try to describe what data it must have learned from.
Write the question first. Then decide what single piece of data would answer it. Only then design the form.

items: What exactly are you measuring?
Who is being asked, and did they agree?
What will you do with a blank answer?

body.text: Before modelling, know the shape of what you have: how many rows, how many columns, what is missing and what is impossible.

body.source:
rows = 240
missing_age = 12
print("rows:", rows)
print("missing age:", missing_age, "->", round(missing_age / rows * 100, 1), "%")

body.text: A model that predicts "not fraud" every time is 99% accurate on a dataset where 1% is fraud, and completely useless. Always ask what the model is accurate at.
The people who built and deployed the system. "The computer decided" has never been a complete answer, and it will not become one.
If you cannot explain why a system produced a decision, think hard before letting it make that decision about a person.

questions.text: Which is the clearest sign a system is using AI?
options: It runs on a fast computer
It improves at a task from data
It is connected to the internet
questions.explanation: Learning from data is the distinguishing feature.

questions.text: Which stage of the AI project cycle comes first?
questions.explanation: You cannot collect the right data until you know the problem.

questions.text: A model works poorly for one group of people. The most likely cause is:
options: Training data that did not include them
questions.explanation: A model reproduces the pattern in its training data.

questions.text: Data you collect yourself for your own project is called:
questions.explanation: Primary is first-hand; secondary was collected by someone else.

questions.text: A survey records an age of 250. The right first action is to:
options: Treat it as an error and record it as missing
questions.explanation: Record the correction; never silently invent a plausible value.

questions.text: Marks are 12, 14, 15, 16 and 98. Which is true?
options: The mean describes the class well
The median describes the class better than the mean
questions.explanation: One extreme value drags the mean but barely moves the median.

questions.text: A bar chart whose axis starts at 90 rather than 0 will:
questions.explanation: A truncated axis exaggerates. Read the scale first.
